headline: Oil gave back an early jump after the US let some blacklisted tankers unload, leaving most currencies flat. The pound held near $1.34 on hot UK inflation, and France's 10-year borrowing cost topped 5%.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: The dollar index ended flat near 101.7, close to a three-week low. Oil's morning jump on Iran's hard line faded in the afternoon, and a weak US 20-year bond sale barely moved yields, so the dollar had little reason to move.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: since the US–Iran war began in February, high oil has kept US inflation up, and with it bets that the Federal Reserve raises rates again in December, which supports the dollar. Talk of peace proposals earlier this week pulled the dollar to a three-week low. What changed: Iran's refusal to send its enriched uranium abroad lifted oil in the morning, but the gain faded after the US Treasury let some cargo come off tankers it had just blacklisted, and the dollar eased back. Official figures showed another big drop in US crude stocks. A sale of 20-year US government bonds went at a record yield with weak foreign demand, yet the 10-year Treasury yield ended near 5.1%, about unchanged. Bets on the Fed did not move: a hold on October 28 is the strong favourite and a December hike is about 90% priced. What it means: the dollar is moving with oil and the war headlines, not with US data. The question to keep asking: does oil stay high enough to keep the Fed's December hike on the table?
chapters.fx: What's next: weekly US jobless claims Thursday at 7:30 AM CT (about 200,000 expected) and the US leading index at 9:00 AM CT. The Fed stays in its quiet period, with no speeches, until its October 28 decision.
numbers: Fed: Oct 28 hold ~84–85%; Dec hike ~90% (CME FedWatch)
US 20-year bond sale at 5.469%, a record for that maturity

scenarios.base: If oil stays near $110 and jobless claims stay low, the dollar holds near 101.7.
scenarios.bull: If Gulf fighting escalates and oil jumps again, US yields rise and the dollar recovers.
scenarios.bear: If a real opening in US–Iran talks drains oil, yields fall and the dollar slips to new lows for the month.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro ended flat near $1.123. France's 10-year borrowing cost rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, and euro-area gas prices topped €90 per megawatt-hour, both weighing on the euro ahead of Moody's review of France on Friday.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the euro has been held back by France's budget fight and by expensive energy, which Europe imports. The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, because euro-area inflation is running near 3.8%. What changed: France's 10-year bond yield rose above 5%, its highest since 2002, and the gap over German yields is the widest since the euro debt crisis. Euro-area natural gas prices rose above €90 per megawatt-hour for the first time since late 2022, and German producer prices came in hotter than expected. The euro held near $1.123 against the dollar but stayed close to its weakest against the pound in 17 months. What it means: a likely December ECB hike supports the euro, but France's borrowing costs and the energy bill pull the other way, and for now they are winning. The question: does Moody's cut France's credit rating on Friday?
chapters.fx: What's next: euro-area consumer confidence Thursday at 9:00 AM CT. Friday: Moody's review of France's credit rating. October 27: the French parliament's revenue vote. October 29: the ECB's decision.

scenarios.bull: If oil eases or ECB officials firm up a December hike, the euro gains.
scenarios.bear: If Moody's cuts France or French yields keep climbing, the euro slips.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: The pound closed near $1.34, holding its gain after UK inflation hit 3.5% in September, above the 3.4% forecast. A Bank of England hike on November 5 is close to fully priced and a second in December is about a coin toss. Governor Andrew Bailey said nothing new on rates.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Gulf war has pushed up energy bills, and Britain, which imports a lot of gas, has felt it more than most. The Bank of England has held rates at 3.75%, but strong jobs figures on Tuesday made a November hike likely. What changed: UK consumer prices, which measure how much prices rose over the past year, came in at 3.5% for September, up from 3.1% and above the 3.4% forecast, with services at 3.7%. That is far above the Bank's 2% target, and motor fuel did most of the lifting, so the energy shock is still feeding into prices. For the pound, that makes a November hike to 4% look almost certain and a second hike in December roughly a 50–50 bet, which keeps UK rates high and supports sterling. Governor Andrew Bailey's appearance at 8:00 AM CT brought no new signal on rates. UK house prices and September government borrowing both came in weaker than hoped, a week before the budget. What it means: November is settled; the debate is now December. The question: how long does the Bank think energy will keep inflation up?
chapters.fx: What's next: UK consumer confidence Thursday at 6:01 PM CT. October 28: the UK budget, which may add help with energy bills. November 5: the Bank of England's decision.
numbers: UK CPI 3.5% y/y (3.4% expected; 3.1% in August); services 3.7%
BoE: Nov 5 hike ~95–98%; Dec second hike ~51%

scenarios.base: If the budget avoids big surprises, the pound holds near $1.34 into November 5.
scenarios.bull: If Bank of England officials open the door to a December follow-up, UK yields and the pound rise.
scenarios.bear: If officials call the energy jump temporary, December bets fade and the pound gives back some gains.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The yen ended flat near 158.2 per dollar. Reports that the Bank of Japan will raise its inflation forecasts next week kept a December hike in view, with odds near 80%, but high oil and the wide gap with US rates held the yen back.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the yen has been weak because US interest rates are far above Japan's, and because Japan pays more for imported energy when oil is high. The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30 and is seen raising rates in December. What changed: Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino said underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal, and a former senior Bank of Japan official said he expects a December hike, nudging those odds up to about 80% from about 73%. Reports that the bank will lift its inflation forecasts next week kept a lid on the dollar against the yen. Oil's morning jump pulled the other way, and the yen ended about where it started. What it means: a likely December hike helps the yen, but the oil bill and the gap with US rates keep it stuck near 158. The question: does Japan's inflation figure, out Thursday evening CT, keep December on track?
chapters.fx: What's next: Japan's national inflation figures for September Thursday at 6:30 PM CT (2.1% expected for the core measure, from 1.7%). October 29–30: the Bank of Japan's meeting.
numbers: Japan core CPI expected 2.1% (1.7% prior), Thu 6:30 PM CT

scenarios.bull: If Japan's inflation figure comes in hot, December hike bets firm and the yen gains.
scenarios.bear: If oil climbs further and US yields rise, the yen weakens toward 159.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The franc ended flat near 0.825 per dollar with no Swiss news. Iran's hard line and France's rising borrowing costs did not set off a rush into safe havens.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the franc is a safe place to park money in uncertain times, and with fighting in the Gulf and France's budget trouble it has been strong against the euro. The Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero and could cut in December because Swiss inflation is very low. What changed: nothing Swiss. Tension in the Gulf rose and French yields climbed, but neither sparked a scramble for safety, so the franc barely moved. What it means: the franc's strength comes from worry elsewhere, not from Switzerland. The question: does fear in the Gulf or in France rise enough to push it further?
chapters.fx: What's next: the SNB's summary of its September policy discussion Thursday at 2:30 AM CT, a read on how worried it is about the strong franc. The next SNB decision is December 10.

scenarios.base: Without a new scare, the franc stays firm against the euro and moves with the dollar.
scenarios.bull: A Gulf escalation or French bond stress sends money into the franc.
scenarios.bear: If the SNB's summary warns about the franc's strength, it gives back some ground against the euro.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Aussie rose about 0.25% to near 70.3 US cents, a three-week high and the best showing among major currencies today. A warning on inflation from Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser lifted the odds of a November hike to about 42%.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Reserve Bank of Australia has raised rates four times this year to 4.60% as inflation stays sticky, and that has made the Aussie one of the stronger major currencies. What changed: the Aussie rose for a fourth day. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser called the inflation outlook materially worse, partly because of oil, and markets now give a November 3 hike about a 42% chance, up from about 30% at the start of the week. Goldman Sachs switched to forecasting a November hike, and a soft US dollar helped too. What it means: the RBA's tone is the main support for the Aussie, and the case now rests on one number. The question: does next week's inflation report justify a fifth hike?
chapters.fx: What's next: Australia's October flash business surveys (PMIs) Thursday at 5:00 PM CT. October 28: Australia's third-quarter inflation report, the deciding number. November 2–3: the RBA's decision.

scenarios.base: If the dollar stays soft and the RBA's tone holds, the Aussie stays near 70 cents.
scenarios.bull: If more RBA officials echo Hauser, November hike bets climb and the Aussie extends.
scenarios.bear: If the risk mood sours on the Gulf, the Aussie gives back its gains.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The loonie ended flat near 1.406 per US dollar, close to its strongest in a month. Bets on a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28 firmed to about 93%, but US crude fell as Washington lent out emergency fuel, which held the loonie back.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: the Bank of Canada was expected to hold until Governor Tiff Macklem warned on October 17 that its inflation forecast will be revised substantially higher because of energy. Markets swung toward an October 28 hike, and Alberta's vote this week to stay in Canada removed a political worry. What changed: hike bets firmed to about 93% in swaps, though strategists at Brown Brothers Harriman argued this week that markets expect too many hikes. US crude, the benchmark closest to Canada's oil, fell for a second day as Washington lent out emergency heating oil and crude, so the loonie stayed flat. What it means: a hike is mostly in the price already, so the loonie needs more than a hike to rise much further, and a surprise hold would hit it. The question: does the Bank of Canada deliver what markets expect?
chapters.fx: What's next: Canadian producer and raw-material prices Thursday at 7:30 AM CT. October 28: the Bank of Canada's decision, with its new forecasts.

scenarios.base: If hike bets hold and oil stays high, the loonie stays near its one-month best.
scenarios.bull: If oil climbs again, the loonie extends its gains.
scenarios.bear: If oil drops on a peace opening or Bank of Canada officials cool hike talk, the loonie slips.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi held near 57 US cents ahead of New Zealand's third-quarter inflation report at 4:45 PM CT tonight. Markets give a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 about an 80% chance, and this figure decides it.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: New Zealand's central bank has been debating whether to raise rates again on October 28. Business activity is strong and dairy prices firmed this week, but parts of the economy are soft. What changed: nothing new from New Zealand; the kiwi drifted as traders waited for the inflation report. What it means: with a hike about 80% priced, a figure near forecast mostly keeps the kiwi where it is, while a clearly soft one would revive talk of a hold. The question: does inflation cool as much as expected?
chapters.fx: What's next: New Zealand's third-quarter inflation report at 4:45 PM CT tonight (about 3.8% a year expected, from 4.1%; about 0.8% for the quarter). October 28: the RBNZ's decision.

scenarios.base: If inflation lands near 3.8%, hike bets hold and the kiwi stays near 57 cents.
scenarios.bull: If inflation comes in hot, the hike looks settled and the kiwi rises.
scenarios.bear: If inflation comes in well below forecast, hold talk returns and the kiwi falls.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Brent crude ended flat at $108.82 a barrel after rising above $110 in the morning. Iran's hard line and another big drop in US crude stocks lifted prices; a US Treasury licence letting some blacklisted tankers unload, and emergency fuel loans, pulled them back.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: since the US–Iran war began in February, oil has carried a large risk premium, and attacks on Gulf shipping pushed Brent to a five-month high near $112 on Tuesday. What changed: Iran's top security official said none of Iran's enriched uranium will leave the country, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called a deal extremely difficult, and the US sent another carrier group, so Brent rose about $2 to near $110.85. Official US figures then showed crude stocks fell 3.1 million barrels last week, far more than expected and a third weekly fall in a row. In the afternoon the US Treasury allowed some cargo to come off tankers it had just blacklisted, and the government said it will lend out a third of its Northeast heating-oil reserve, and prices gave back the gain. US crude fell 0.7% to $97.15. What it means: diplomacy is stuck and supply is tight, but Washington is working to cap fuel prices before the November 3 elections. That tug of war keeps oil high but jumpy, supporting exporters like the Canadian dollar and costing importers like the euro and yen. The question: does Washington's push to ease supply outweigh the attacks on shipping?
chapters.fx: What's next: OPEC+ meets on November 1. Any confirmed opening in US–Iran talks would cut the premium quickly; a strike on a major loading site would add to it.

scenarios.bull: If a major loading site or tanker route is hit, Brent tops Tuesday's $112 high.
scenarios.bear: If Washington eases more sanctions or talks open up, the premium drains and Brent falls toward $106.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold ended a touch lower near $4,120–4,135 an ounce after bouncing at midday when oil slipped. Bets near 90% on a December Federal Reserve hike, and US 10-year yields above 5%, keep weighing on a metal that pays no interest.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: gold rallied to a record above $5,600 in January on war and inflation fears, but rising interest rates have weighed on it since. What changed: gold slipped in the morning as oil jumped, since higher oil strengthens the case for more rate hikes. It bounced to about $4,133 when the US Treasury's tanker licence pulled oil lower and bonds rallied, then settled back, with December futures down about 0.2%. What it means: higher rates are beating fear right now. Gold needs either falling yields or a real shock to turn up. The question: do US yields keep climbing?
chapters.fx: What's next: weekly US jobless claims Thursday at 7:30 AM CT. Gulf headlines and US 10-year yields drive gold in the meantime.

scenarios.base: If yields hold above 5%, gold drifts within its range.
scenarios.bull: A big Gulf escalation or a sharp drop in yields brings buyers back.
scenarios.bear: If yields climb further on oil-led inflation fears, gold extends its losing run.
